title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its level order traversal, meaning the node values grouped level by level from top to bottom, left to right within each level.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal — BFS with queue

s1_definition.profdef: Level order traversal visits a binary tree breadth-first, one level at a time from top to bottom and left to right within each level. It uses a queue: you enqueue the root, then repeatedly process all nodes currently in the queue as one level, collecting their values and enqueuing their children for the next level.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to read the bank's org chart rank by rank, first the branch manager alone, then all the direct reports together, then all of their reports together, and so on. He keeps a line of people to visit. He notes how many are in the line right now, processes exactly that many as one rank, and as he does, he adds each person's own reports to the back of the line for the next rank.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use a queue, and at each step process exactly the number of nodes currently queued to capture one full level before moving down.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Level order traversal visits a binary tree breadth-first, one level at a time from top to bottom and left to right within each level. It uses a queue: you enqueue the root, then repeatedly process all nodes currently in the queue as one level, collecting their values and enqueuing their children for the next level.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants to read the bank's org chart rank by rank, first the branch manager alone, then all the direct reports together, then all of their reports together, and so on. He keeps a line of people to visit. He notes how many are in the line right now, processes exactly that many as one rank, and as he does, he adds each person's own reports to the back of the line for the next rank.

**One line to remember:** Use a queue, and at each step process exactly the number of nodes currently queued to capture one full level before moving down.

sections.s2_technical:
Breadth-first traversal naturally uses a First-In-First-Out queue, because you want to visit nodes in the order they were discovered. The key technique that groups output by level is capturing the queue's size at the start of each level.

You begin by enqueuing the root if it is not null. For example: `if (root != null) queue.offer(root);`.

Then you loop while the queue is not empty. At the start of each iteration you record the current size, which is exactly the number of nodes on this level. For example: `int levelSize = queue.size();`. You then dequeue precisely that many nodes, collect their values into a list for this level, and enqueue their non-null children. For example: `for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) { Node n = queue.poll(); level.add(n.value); if (n.left != null) queue.offer(n.left); if (n.right != null) queue.offer(n.right); }`.

After the inner loop, the level list holds one full level in left-to-right order, which you add to the result. For example: `result.add(level);`.

The time complexity is linear because each node is enqueued and dequeued once. The space complexity is proportional to the maximum width of the tree, because the queue at its fullest holds one entire level. A senior nuance is that capturing the level size up front is what cleanly separates levels; without it you cannot tell where one level ends and the next begins. Many variations build on this base, such as zigzag order, right-side view, or averages per level, all driven by the same size-snapshot technique.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the compliance team wants to view the loan approval hierarchy rank by rank, so they can see all approvers at the same authority level together. A depth-first dump would interleave levels confusingly. This is exactly how Level Order Traversal works — it reports each authority rank as its own group.

Problem 2 — The report must preserve left-to-right order within a rank, because that encodes seniority within a level. This is exactly why BFS with a queue, processing a fixed count per level, keeps the order correct.

The mini-project builds an `ApproverNode` class, a `HierarchyLevelService` with a `levelOrder` method using a queue and logging, and a runnable demo that prints each rank of a sample hierarchy.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the hierarchy rooted at Manager.

Step 1: Manager is enqueued. The queue holds Manager.

Step 2: The loop starts. The level size is one. It dequeues Manager, adds Manager to the level list, and enqueues its children CreditOfficer and RiskHead. The level list is Manager, which becomes rank zero. The queue now holds CreditOfficer and RiskHead.

Step 3: The level size is two. It dequeues CreditOfficer, adds it, and enqueues its children JrA and JrB. It dequeues RiskHead, adds it, and enqueues its child RegionalVP. The level list is CreditOfficer, RiskHead, which becomes rank one. The queue now holds JrA, JrB, RegionalVP.

Step 4: The level size is three. It dequeues JrA, JrB, and RegionalVP in order, adding each to the level list. None of them have children. The level list is JrA, JrB, RegionalVP, which becomes rank two. The queue is now empty.

Step 5: The queue is empty, so the loop ends. The result has three ranks, logged in order.

```text
2026-10-26T18:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Approval Hierarchy by Rank
2026-10-26T18:00:00Z [INFO] Rank 0: [Manager]
2026-10-26T18:00:00Z [INFO] Rank 1: [CreditOfficer, RiskHead]
2026-10-26T18:00:00Z [INFO] Rank 2: [JrA, JrB, RegionalVP]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  queue: [Manager]
    │ levelSize=1 → poll Manager; enqueue Credit,Risk
    ▼ rank0 = [Manager]
  queue: [CreditOfficer, RiskHead]
    │ levelSize=2 → poll both; enqueue JrA,JrB,RegionalVP
    ▼ rank1 = [CreditOfficer, RiskHead]
  queue: [JrA, JrB, RegionalVP]
    │ levelSize=3 → poll all; no children
    ▼ rank2 = [JrA, JrB, RegionalVP]
  queue: [] → done
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Level order traversal is a breadth-first walk of the tree, and the natural data structure for breadth-first is a First-In-First-Out queue, because I want to visit nodes in the order they were discovered. I enqueue the root, then loop while the queue is not empty, and the single technique that groups the output cleanly by level is snapshotting the queue's size at the start of each iteration.

That size snapshot tells me exactly how many nodes belong to the current level. I dequeue precisely that many, collect their values into a list for this level, and as I process each one I enqueue its non-null children, which populates the queue for the next level. When the inner loop finishes, the level list holds one full rank in left-to-right order, and I add it to the result. Without that size snapshot I could not tell where one level ends and the next begins.

The time complexity is linear because every node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once, and the space is proportional to the maximum width of the tree, since at its fullest the queue holds one entire level. This base pattern is also the foundation for many variations like zigzag order, right-side view, or per-level averages, all of which reuse the same size-snapshot loop.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this to produce a rank-by-rank view of the loan approval hierarchy for the compliance dashboard, so reviewers can see all approvers at the same authority level grouped together. Preserving the left-to-right order within each rank was important because it encodes seniority within a level, and the queue-based traversal with a fixed count per level kept both the grouping and the ordering correct.
